new.definition: A large bird native to North America, Meleagris gallopavo, and the center of the American Thanksgiving table. Its breast and wings are white meat and its legs and thighs are dark meat: color in muscle comes mainly from myoglobin, a protein that stores oxygen, and a turkey rarely flies, so its breast stays pale while its working legs turn dark. White meat is lean and dries out when overcooked, while dark meat is richer and takes well to slow cooking. Food safety guidance calls for the bird, and any stuffing, to reach 165 °F.
new.guest: Turkey is the bird at the heart of the American Thanksgiving table, and it is native to this continent. On Thanksgiving Day we served it two ways: the lean white breast brined in buttermilk and roasted, and the richer dark leg braised slowly until tender, so white meat and dark meat lovers each had their favorite.
new.kitchen: Breast and leg cook best apart: the breast comes out once it reaches a safe 165 °F so it stays moist, while the leg is given a long, gentle, covered cook. How long the kitchen brined, roasted and braised was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Chicken is the nearest neighbor: both are poultry with white breast meat and dark leg meat, but a turkey is a far larger bird, so its breast and legs are more often cooked apart, as they were on the Thanksgiving plate.

new.background: The wild turkey is native to North America. It was domesticated in Mexico at least two thousand years ago, and a second domestication in the American Southwest later died out, so the turkeys raised today descend from the Mexican bird. Spanish ships carried it to Europe around 1500, and within about a century it had spread across the continent; European colonists later brought domestic turkeys back across the Atlantic to the eastern colonies. Its English name is often explained as a mix up with the guinea fowl, which reached Europe through Turkish traders, though linguists say the origin is not settled. In 1863 Abraham Lincoln (1809 to 1865) proclaimed a national Thanksgiving for the last Thursday in November, after a long campaign by a writer who had appealed to him by letter that September.

new.definition: French for juice: on a menu, a light sauce made from the juices a roast gives up as it cooks, often reduced to concentrate its flavor. It is thinner and clearer than a flour gravy. Served unthickened, the meat is said to come au jus, in its own juice; thickened lightly with a starch such as arrowroot or cornstarch, it becomes a jus lié. The turkey on the Thanksgiving Day menu came with a cranberry and rosemary jus.
new.guest: A jus, said zhoo, is a light sauce made from the roast’s own juices, thinner and brighter than a flour gravy, so it seasons the meat without weighing it down. Ours on Thanksgiving Day carried tart cranberry and piney rosemary for the turkey.
new.kitchen: The kitchen builds a jus from the pan juices and stock, reduces it for flavor and strains it; a little starch slurry turns it into a jus lié. Whether the cranberry and rosemary jus was thickened at all was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Gravy is the nearest neighbor: a gravy is thickened, usually with flour, and coats the meat, while a jus is thin and glossy, and even a jus lié is thickened only lightly with a clear starch.

new.background: The word goes back to the Latin ius, broth, sauce or juice, which became jus in Old French; the English word juice comes from the same root by another road. In the French kitchen a jus is the natural juice a meat releases as it cooks, and the word has also named a clear or lightly thickened brown stock, especially of veal. A jus lié is a brown stock or jus thickened lightly with arrowroot or cornstarch,. American menus took up the phrase au jus for beef served with its own juices, and it is tied above all to the French dip sandwich, roast beef on a roll dipped in jus, which two Los Angeles restaurants, Philippe’s and Cole’s, each claim to have invented early in the twentieth century.

new.definition: The tart red berry of the American cranberry, Vaccinium macrocarpon, a plant of the bogs and wetlands of North America. Each berry holds four small air pockets, so it floats, and growers gather most of the crop by flooding the beds, knocking the berries loose and skimming them from the surface. Raw the fruit is sharply sour; cooked with sugar it becomes the bright sauce of the holiday table. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it came as a side of cranberry sauce and in the turkey’s jus.
new.guest: Cranberries are native to North America, gathered here by Native peoples long before the colonists came, and they are harvested in the fall, just in time for Thanksgiving. Our cranberry sauce was tart and bright, made to cut through the richness of the turkey, and the turkey’s own jus carried cranberry too.
new.kitchen: Cranberries are cooked with sugar until the berries burst and soften into a sauce. The house recipe, and whether the sauce was left whole or made smooth, was a question for lineup.
new.compare: A cranberry relish is the nearest neighbor: a relish is usually ground raw with sugar, so it stays coarse and sharp, while a sauce is cooked until the berries burst and turn soft and glossy.

new.background: Native peoples gathered the cranberry long before Europeans arrived: pounded with dried deer meat and fat into pemmican, it made a food that kept for months on long journeys, and the berries also served as a dye. The English name is usually traced to craneberry, for the likeness of the flower to the head and bill of a crane. Cultivation began in Dennis, Massachusetts, in 1816 by most accounts, when a grower saw that his wild vines grew better where sand blew over them. American Cookery, printed in 1796 and held to be the first cookbook written by an American, already recommended cranberry sauce with roast turkey, though it gave no recipe. In 1912 a Massachusetts grower began canning cranberry sauce to stretch the short selling season, and his venture later grew into the Ocean Spray cooperative.

new.definition: A savory mixture of bread with broth, aromatics and seasoning, baked in its own pan beside the bird rather than inside it. In the South it is most often made with crumbled cornbread, and cooks add their own touches, such as sausage, oysters or pecans. Stuffing is the name for the same kind of mixture cooked inside the bird, though in everyday speech the words cross, and the South and Midwest tend to say dressing. On the Thanksgiving Day menu cornbread dressing came with the turkey.
new.guest: Dressing is the Southern way with stuffing: crumbled cornbread with broth, aromatics and herbs, baked in its own pan rather than inside the bird. Ours came with the Thanksgiving turkey, and for the table there was also Titus’ BBQ Shrimp Stuffing, a New Orleans turn on the same idea.
new.kitchen: Baked apart from the bird, the dressing browns on top and cooks through on its own; food safety guidance asks that any stuffing reach 165 °F at its center. What went into the house cornbread dressing was a question for lineup, so never guess at sausage or oysters.
new.compare: Stuffing is its nearest neighbor: stuffing is cooked inside the bird and dressing is baked in its own pan, but in the South dressing is often the word for both, so ask how it was cooked, not what it was called.

new.background: Cornbread, the base of the Southern dressing, is a quick bread of cornmeal with its origins in Native American cooking. In the South, enslaved cooks given cornmeal as a ration made kush, cornbread mashed with onions and served with gravy, a dish some food historians count as a forerunner of baked cornbread dressing, with roots reaching back to the grain dishes of West Africa. The names now split by region: the Northeast tends to say stuffing, the South and Midwest dressing. A popular story holds that the Victorians preferred dressing because stuffing sounded crude, but the record does not prove it, and where the split began is hard to say.

deepen.background: Chefs have long soaked lean meats such as poultry in salted water so they would not dry out, but brining reached home Thanksgiving cooks in a wave only around the end of the 1990s, when newspapers and television cooking shows carried turkey brines to a wide audience. Food science explains the effect: a salt solution dissolves part of the protein structure inside muscle fibers, so the meat takes up brine and holds on to more water, and a brined breast loses less of its juice in the oven. Southern cooks have their own brine in buttermilk, soaking chicken before frying, and its lactic acid tenderizes the meat more gently than vinegar or citrus.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Roasted Buttermilk-Brined Turkey Breast
deepen.guest: Brined means the meat rested in salted liquid before it was cooked, which seasons it right through and helps it stay juicy. On Thanksgiving Day our turkey breast was brined in buttermilk, which adds a gentle tang to the salt.

deepen.background: Buttermilk began as the thin liquid left in the churn after butter was made from cultured cream, and before the 1900s the name covered several drinks, from that by product to plain soured milk. In the 1920s American dairies began adding cultures to milk and selling the result as buttermilk, and that cultured product, thicker and more acidic than the churned kind, is what stores sell today. Its acid reacts with baking soda, which made it the classic liquid of Southern biscuits; churned buttermilk is thinner and less acidic and does not act on soda the same way. Southern cooks also soak chicken in it before frying, because its lactic acid tenderizes the meat gently.

deepen.guest: Buttermilk is cultured milk with a gentle, tangy flavor, the same buttermilk behind Southern biscuits and fried chicken. On Thanksgiving Day our turkey breast was brined in it, which seasons the meat and leaves a soft tang.

deepen.background: Roasting is among the oldest ways of cooking: from prehistory people held meat over an open fire, and for centuries a roast meant meat turned on a spit before the flames. Cooking meat by dry heat in a closed oven was long called baking, and the Oxford English Dictionary treats bake as the original word for oven cooking; roast followed the meat into the oven later, and the old line between the two words was clearer before modern kitchen appliances. The English word came from the Old French rostir, of Germanic origin. Today the two words overlap in ordinary kitchens, though roasting usually describes meats and vegetables browned in the dry heat of the oven, and baking breads, cakes and pastries.

deepen.guest: Roasted means cooked in the dry heat of the oven, so the outside browns and the flavor deepens while the inside stays juicy. On Thanksgiving Day that was the buttermilk brined turkey breast, the herb roasted beef tenderloin and its Brussels sprouts, and the apples with the pork.

deepen.background: The word is French: braiser is formed from braise, live coals or embers, from an Old French word probably of Germanic origin, and it entered English in the second half of the eighteenth century. The name records how braising was first done. On the open hearth the cook nestled a tightly lidded pan, the braisière, into the embers and heaped more hot coals into the rim of its lid, so the heat came from above and below at once. Later pots kept the shape: the recessed lid of the doufeu first held embers, and the colonial Dutch oven had a flanged lid to keep coals out of the food.

deepen.guest: Braised means browned and then cooked slowly, covered, in a little liquid until it is tender, and that liquid becomes the sauce. On Thanksgiving Day the turkey leg was braised for rich, tender dark meat beside the roast breast.
